passage:
Dear Charu Ma'am,
You once told me to check my own patterns, so here is a confession. Last month I looked at the task tracker for my team of four. Every tricky client problem had gone to Ankit. Every routine data-cleaning job had gone to Farzana. I never decided that on purpose. It just felt natural, because Ankit "seemed quick" in his first week.
So I changed it. This month all four get one hard problem each, the same fifteen-minute feedback chat every Friday, and the same patience when they ask questions. I'm judging by what they deliver, not by my first impression.
Two weeks in, Farzana's fix for a billing issue was the best in the team. I nearly never found out.
Gratefully,
Rekha

qa.q: What kind of jobs had gone to Farzana?
qa.a: Every routine data-cleaning job.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on finding that Farzana's fix was the best, and why?
qa.a: Rekha seems relieved and a little shaken ("I nearly never found out"), realising the old pattern would have hidden what Farzana could do.

qa.q: Which changes did Rekha make, and why are they fair?
qa.a: All four now get one hard problem, the same Friday feedback chat and the same patience, and are judged by what they deliver, so no first impression decides anyone's chances.

qa.q: How might Farzana have experienced the months before the change?
qa.a: Farzana kept getting routine jobs without knowing why, and may have felt stuck or overlooked, with no chance to show what Farzana could do.

grounding: A young manager notices hard tasks went to one person and routine ones to another, then gives everyone the same challenge, feedback and patience.

passage: Honestly? What surprised me most in my first year as kitchen manager was me. I'm Deepika, twenty-five, and I run the kitchen at a hotel in Kochi. For months I gave the new dishes to Suresh and the chopping to Farida. When a sauce went wrong, I'd explain it patiently to Suresh and just fix it myself for Farida. One night I watched her standing by the prep counter while Suresh plated my new fish curry, and I thought: when did I decide she couldn't? I had no evidence. So I made a rule. Everyone rotates through the new dishes, everyone gets the same tasting feedback, and I write down what actually happens. Farida's first attempt was average. Her third was the best version we've served.

qa.q: Where does Deepika run the kitchen?
qa.a: At a hotel in Kochi.

qa.q: What was Deepika thinking while watching Farida at the prep counter?
qa.a: Deepika wondered when the decision that Farida couldn't handle new dishes had been made, and realised there was no evidence for it. 🤔

qa.q: Which rule did Deepika make, and why does writing things down matter?
qa.a: Everyone rotates through new dishes with the same tasting feedback, and Deepika records results; writing down what happens means judging by evidence, not impressions.

qa.q: How might the kitchen feel different to Farida after the rotation?
qa.a: Farida finally gets new dishes and real feedback instead of only chopping, so the kitchen can become a place to grow, and her third attempt shows it.

grounding: A young kitchen manager notices a habit of giving new dishes to one cook and chopping to another, then gives everyone the same chances and judges by results.

passage: I'm Jasleen, and I've worked under Rajni at the call centre for a year. In her team meeting last Monday, she did something I've never seen a manager do. She put up the list of who had handled the escalation calls: nine to Varun, none to Gulnaz. Then she said, "I didn't plan that. I think I just expected more from Varun. That isn't fair." From that day, escalations rotate, and each of us gets the same ten minutes of feedback after a hard call. When Gulnaz fumbled her first escalation, Rajni didn't take it back; she listened to the recording with her and let her try again. I don't know what Gulnaz felt, but she asks questions in meetings now, which she never did before.

qa.q: How many escalation calls had gone to Gulnaz?
qa.a: None.

qa.q: Why do you think Rajni showed the list to the whole team?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable with an unfair pattern she hadn't planned, and wanted to fix it openly so everyone knew things would change.

qa.q: What choice did Rajni make when Gulnaz fumbled her first escalation, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She didn't take the calls back; she went through the recording with Gulnaz and let her try again, giving her the same patience others had got.

qa.q: How might Varun feel about the change?
qa.a: Varun loses some hard calls and the quiet special status, which might sting a little, though the same fair feedback now applies to Varun as well.

grounding: A colleague watches a young manager admit she gave hard calls to one person and none to another, then rotate them with equal feedback and patience.

passage:
Monday: Jeevan, twenty-six and newly made site supervisor, sat with the weekly plan for the housing project in Nashik. Slab inspection: Arvind. Structural checks: Arvind. Paperwork and material register: Rashmi. He frowned. Rashmi had the same degree and the same six months on site. Why had he done that? He couldn't find a reason, only a feeling.
Three weeks later: he rotated the plan. Rashmi got the third-floor slab inspection. She missed a crack near a column, and Jeevan walked her to it and explained, slowly, the way he always did with Arvind. She wrote it down and thanked him.
Two months later: at the review, Jeevan pulled out the inspection logs instead of trusting his impressions. Rashmi's were the most detailed on the site. Arvind's were good but rushed. Jeevan put both names on the next tower and wrote in his notebook: check the list, not the feeling.

qa.q: What did Rashmi miss during her first slab inspection?
qa.a: She missed a crack near a column.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when he looked at the weekly plan on Monday?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, frowning when he saw he had given Arvind all the tough work for no reason but a feeling, though Rashmi had the same degree and experience.

qa.q: Which of Jeevan's choices made the plan fairer, and why?
qa.a: He rotated the tough tasks, gave Rashmi the same patient explanation he gave Arvind, and judged them later by their logs, not his impressions.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have seen the change in her work?
qa.a: Rashmi probably felt trusted and taken seriously for the first time, getting real inspections and patient feedback instead of only paperwork.

grounding: A young site supervisor notices he hands tough work to one engineer and routine work to another, then gives both the same challenge and patience and judges by the logs.

passage: Parul, you've just been made team lead and you're asking me how to be fair. Let old Vasudha tell you her mistake. At twenty-five I was made head of the primary section at a school in Indore, the youngest in the staffroom. That first year, I gave the science exhibition, the inspection lessons and the parents' meetings to Mrs Joshi, because she spoke well. Mrs Rao got the attendance and the timetable. In March I made the list for the annual report and saw it written down. I felt quite ashamed. I had never once watched Mrs Rao teach. So the next year, I made a rotation. Everyone got a big project, everyone got my notes, everyone got the same patience when things went wrong. And I looked at results, children's work, not at who sounded confident. Mrs Rao's class did the best model at the exhibition. Write your list down, Parul. The list doesn't lie.

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao's class do at the next exhibition?
qa.a: Mrs Rao's class did the best model at the exhibition.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel on seeing the list written down?
qa.a: Vasudha felt quite ashamed, seeing that one teacher had got everything big and the other only routine work, without ever being watched teaching.

qa.q: What changes did Vasudha make, and how can Parul use them?
qa.a: Vasudha rotated the big projects, gave everyone the same notes and patience, and judged by children's work; Parul can write down the team's task list and do the same.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt in that first year?
qa.a: Mrs Rao may have felt overlooked and underused, handling attendance and timetables while someone else got all the chances to shine.

grounding: A retired head tells a new lead how they once noticed giving the big tasks to one teacher and routine work to another, then gave all the same challenge and judged by results.
